methods.returns: a list of text, one character per item
notes: ToList and Chars return the same list

methods.name: ToList
methods.brief: Returns the held characters as a plain list, one single-character text per item.
notes: same answer as Content, under a name that says the type

methods.name: Chars
methods.brief: Returns the held characters as a plain list, one single-character text per item.
notes: same answer as Content, under the name used when a text is split into characters

methods.name: Names
methods.brief: Returns the official Unicode name of each character, in order.
methods.returns: a list of text, one name per character
notes: the space is named SPACE and the emoji 😀 is GRINNING FACE

methods.name: RemoveSpaces
methods.brief: RemoveSpaces / RemoveSpacesQ: drop every " " char from the list.

extensions.name: RemoveSpacesQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: Uppercase
methods.brief: Changes every character to its capital form, in place, leaving the other characters as they are.
methods.returns: nothing; the list changes. UppercaseQ returns the object for chaining
notes: works on accented letters too: é becomes É; Hebrew has no capitals and stays as it is

extensions.name: UppercaseQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: Lowercase
methods.brief: Changes every character to its small form, in place, leaving the other characters as they are.

extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

extensions.name: JoinQ

methods.name: Count

methods.name: Section
methods.brief: Returns the characters between two positions, both included, as a list.

parameters.name: p1

parameters.name: p2

methods.returns: a list of text; an empty list when the start is after the end

parameters.name: n

methods.returns: a list of numbers; an empty list when the character is absent

methods.name: Unique
methods.brief: Returns the distinct characters, each kept at its first occurrence, but joined in one text inside a one-item list.
notes: NumberOfUniqueChars counts correctly; RemoveDuplicatesQ returns a proper list of single characters
warnings: the answer is not split into single characters: hello gives [ "helo" ], not [ "h", "e", "l", "o" ], and the same happens for Hebrew, emoji and a list given as input; the engine hands back one text and the splitting finds no separator in it

methods.name: NumberOfUniqueChars
methods.brief: Returns how many different characters the list holds.
notes: hello gives 4

methods.name: SortAsc
methods.brief: Reorders the characters in ascending code point order, in place, but leaves them joined in one item.
notes: Sort does the same
warnings: the list then holds ONE item, the whole sorted text, so NumberOfChars answers 1 afterwards: hello becomes [ "ehllo" ] and not [ "e", "h", "l", "l", "o" ]; the engine hands back one text and the splitting finds no separator in it

methods.name: SortedAsc
methods.brief: Returns the characters in ascending code point order, as a one-item list, leaving the object unchanged.
notes: the same defect as SortAsc
warnings: the answer is one text inside a list: hello gives [ "ehllo" ], not a list of single characters

methods.name: SortDesc
methods.brief: Reorders the characters in descending code point order, in place, but leaves them joined in one item.
notes: the same defect as SortAsc
warnings: the list then holds ONE item, the whole sorted text: hello becomes [ "ollhe" ] and not [ "o", "l", "l", "h", "e" ]; the engine hands back one text and the splitting finds no separator in it

methods.name: SortedDesc
methods.brief: Returns the characters in descending code point order, as a one-item list, leaving the object unchanged.
notes: the same defect as SortAsc
warnings: the answer is one text inside a list: hello gives [ "ollhe" ], not a list of single characters

methods.name: Sort
methods.brief: Reorders the characters in ascending code point order, in place, but leaves them joined in one item.
notes: it calls SortAsc
warnings: the list then holds ONE item, the whole sorted text, exactly as SortAsc does

methods.name: Reverse
methods.brief: Turns the list around, in place, so that the last character comes first.
notes: Hebrew, Arabic and emoji characters stay whole

methods.name: Reversed
methods.brief: Returns the characters in the opposite order as a list, leaving the object unchanged.
notes: a😀b😀 gives 😀, b, 😀, a

methods.name: ToUpper
methods.brief: Changes every character to its capital form, in place, by converting the whole text at once.
notes: the result is split again into single characters, so the list keeps its length

methods.name: Uppercased
methods.brief: Returns the characters in their capital form as a list, leaving the object unchanged.

methods.name: ToLower
methods.brief: Changes every character to its small form, in place, by converting the whole text at once.
notes: the result is split again into single characters, so the list keeps its length

methods.name: Lowercased
methods.brief: Returns the characters in their small form as a list, leaving the object unchanged.

methods.name: Unicodes
methods.brief: Returns the Unicode code point of each character, in order.
notes: the emoji 😀 is 128512 and the Hebrew letter ש is 1513

classes.name: stzStringChecker
classes.brief: Answers yes/no questions about a text: palindrome, anagram, number form, case, composition, marks and regex match.
classes.description: It is the question-answering helper behind many Is... methods of stzString, which builds one over itself and passes the call on; reach for it directly when you only want the checks and not the whole string API. A question answers 1 or 0 and never changes the text. Every question counts characters, not bytes, so a Hebrew or Arabic word and an emoji are one character each. The number checks that expect a prefix (0b, 0o, 0x, U+) answer 0 without it. The case-flag forms (CS) take 1 to compare with case and 0 to ignore it. HasLeadingChars, HasTrailingChars and HasLeadingAndTrailingChars answer 0 for every text today; use the stzString methods of the same names.
classes.example:
? o1.IsPalindrome()
#--> 1
? o1.IsMadeOf([ "lev", "el" ])
#--> 1
o2 = new stzStringChecker("שלום")
? o2.IsReversedCopyOf("םולש")
#--> 1
o3 = new stzStringChecker("a😀b")
? o3.NumberOfChars()
#--> 3

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Builds a checker over a text, given as a string or as a stzString object.

parameters.name: pStrOrStzStrObj
parameters.role: the text to question, or a stzString whose content is questioned (it is held, not copied)

notes: stzString builds one of these for each of its Is... questions

methods.name: Content
methods.brief: Returns the text being questioned, unchanged.

methods.brief: Returns how many characters the text holds, counting an emoji or an accented letter as one.

methods.name: IsPalindrome
methods.brief: TRUE if the text reads the same from the right as from the left, letter case counted.
notes: an empty text is a palindrome; IsPalindromeCS(0) ignores case, so Abba passes with it and fails without it

extensions.name: IsPalindromeCS

parameters.name: pcOtherStr

extensions.name: IsAnagramOfCS

parameters.name: acSubStr

methods.name: RepresentsInteger
methods.brief: TRUE if the text is a whole number, written with an optional leading + or -.
notes: 42, -5 and +5 pass, -3.14 and 0x1F do not

methods.brief: TRUE if the text is a whole number that starts with a + or a - sign.
notes: 42 answers FALSE and -5 answers TRUE

methods.name: RepresentsUnsignedInteger
methods.brief: TRUE if the text is a whole number written without a sign.
notes: 42 answers TRUE and -5 answers FALSE

methods.name: RepresentsNumber
methods.brief: TRUE if the text is a whole or a decimal number, written with an optional leading + or -.
notes: -3.14 and 42 pass, abc does not

methods.name: RepresentsSignedNumber
methods.brief: TRUE if the text is a number, whole or decimal, that starts with a + or a - sign.
notes: -3.14 and +5 answer TRUE, 42 answers FALSE

methods.name: RepresentsUnsignedNumber
methods.brief: TRUE if the text is a number, whole or decimal, written without a sign.
notes: 42 answers TRUE, -3.14 answers FALSE

methods.name: IsListInString
methods.brief: TRUE if the trimmed text starts with a [ and ends with a ], so that it could be read back as a list.
notes: only the two brackets are looked at: the content between them is not parsed

methods.name: RepresentsDecimalNumber
methods.brief: TRUE if the text is a number written with a decimal point, such as 3.14 or -3.14.
notes: 42 answers FALSE: it has no decimal point

methods.name: RepresentsBinaryNumber
methods.brief: TRUE if the text is a 0b or 0B prefix followed by binary digits.
notes: 0b1011 answers TRUE and 1011 answers FALSE: the prefix is required

methods.name: RepresentsHexNumber
methods.brief: TRUE if the text is a 0x or 0X prefix followed by hexadecimal digits.
notes: 0x1F answers TRUE and 1F4a answers FALSE: the prefix is required

methods.name: RepresentsNumberInUnicodeHexForm
methods.brief: TRUE if the text is U+ followed by hexadecimal digits, the way a Unicode code point is written.
notes: U+0041 answers TRUE and 0041 answers FALSE

methods.name: IsCharName
methods.brief: TRUE if the text is the official Unicode name of a character, such as LATIN SMALL LETTER A.
notes: the name is looked up in the engine character database; a letter such as x is not a name

methods.name: IsReversedCopyOf
methods.brief: TRUE if the text is another text read backward, character by character.

parameters.name: pcOtherStr
parameters.role: the text to compare with

notes: works on characters, not bytes: םולש is the reverse of שלום

extensions.name: IsReversedCopyOfCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

methods.name: Reversed
methods.brief: Returns the text with its characters in the opposite order, leaving the checked text unchanged.
notes: an emoji or an accented letter stays whole: a😀b gives b😀a

methods.name: IsChar
methods.brief: TRUE if the text is made of exactly one character.
notes: a letter with a separate combining accent counts as two characters, so it answers FALSE

methods.name: IsLetter
methods.brief: TRUE if the string is a single letter.

methods.name: IsADigit
methods.brief: TRUE if the string is a single digit.

methods.name: IsWord
methods.brief: TRUE if the string is a single word.

methods.name: IsCharsSortedAscending
methods.brief: TRUE if the chars are in ascending order.

methods.name: IsCharsSortedDescending
methods.brief: TRUE if the chars are in descending order.

methods.name: HasLeadingChars
methods.brief: Returns 0 today whatever the text is, instead of telling whether the text starts with a repeated character.
notes: stzString.HasLeadingChars is the working one
warnings: answers FALSE for aab and for xxyy alike: it compares two engine handles, which are never equal, instead of the two characters; the stzString method of the same name answers 1 for aab

methods.name: HasTrailingChars

methods.name: XorEncrypt
methods.brief: XOR with a repeating passphrase, returned as BASE64.
methods.detail: Two bugs lived here. The key was passed as a string HANDLE to an engine function whose key parameter is a single BYTE, so the bridge coerced the pointer to a number and every call XORed with a different arbitrary byte -- "Secret" encrypted and decrypted with "key" came back "Pf`qfw", every byte off by a constant 0x03, the gap between the two accidental keys. And the result is BINARY. Every other cipher here permutes letters and stays in the text domain; XOR does not. The engine's string type validates UTF-8 (rightly), so feeding raw cipher bytes back in for decryption dropped them: "Secret"/"key" happens to produce only ASCII-range bytes and survived, but two Arabic letters produce B5 D0 A1 E0, which is not valid UTF-8, and came back empty. So the cipher now stays inside the engine and what crosses the bridge is always base64. XorDecrypt is a real method rather than an alias for XorEncrypt: the pair is still an involution over the BYTES, but the encoding step has a direction.

classes.name: stzStringEncoder
classes.brief: Turns a text into another representation of itself and back: hexadecimal, binary, octal, code points, URL and HTML escapes, regex escapes and Unicode normal forms.
classes.description: It is the encoding helper behind the encoding methods of stzString (ToHex, UrlEncoded, HtmlDecoded, NormalizedNFC...), which builds one over itself and writes the result back; reach for it directly with new stzStringEncoder(cText) or StzStringEncoderQ(cText) when you only need the encoding. The past-tense forms (UrlEncoded, HtmlDecoded, NormalizedNFC...) return the new text and leave the encoder alone, and the verbs (UrlEncode, FromHex, Reverse...) change the held text in place and return nothing, the Q form returning the encoder so calls chain. Read the result with Content. Note what each form counts: ToHex gives the UTF-8 bytes, ToCharCodes and ToOctal give Unicode code points, and ToBinary gives one group of eight digits per character, which is cut to its low eight bits above code point 255, so it is exact for Latin-1 text only. FromHex does not join UTF-8 bytes back into characters, so it round-trips ASCII only. Pass a plain text, not a stzString object: an edit through an encoder empties the stzString that was passed in.
classes.example:
? o1.ToHex()
#--> 486920c3a9
? o1.UrlEncoded()
#--> Hi%20%C3%A9
? o1.ToCharCodes()
#--> 72 105 32 233
o2 = new stzStringEncoder("שלום")
? o2.UrlEncoded()
#--> %D7%A9%D7%9C%D7%95%D7%9D
? o2.ToCharCodes()
#--> 1513 1500 1493 1501
o3 = new stzStringEncoder("a😀")
? o3.ToHex()
#--> 61f09f9880
? o3.ToCharCodes()
#--> 97 128512

methods.brief: Returns the UTF-8 bytes of the text as lower-case hexadecimal digits, two per byte, with no separator.

methods.brief: Replaces the held text by the text that hexadecimal digits spell, in place, taking each pair of digits as one character.

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Accepts a string, an stzString, OR a bare engine handle (a number).
methods.detail: THE HANDLE FORM EXISTS BECAUSE THE OBJECT FORM COPIES. Ring duplicates an object when it is assigned to an attribute, so `new stzStringFinder(This)` copied the entire string -- and stzString creates a finder per call in 20 methods, making its class surface SLOWER than the bare global functions (26.70 ms vs 12.36 for 200 finds over 180 KB) despite being the side that holds a resident engine handle. Seventeen of this class's uses of @oString are `.Engine()` -- a number. Passing that number directly costs nothing, and the full stzString is rebuilt LAZILY (from the engine's own bytes) only for the handful of methods that need more: Content, NumberOfChars, IsEmpty, StartsWithCS, EndsWithCS, SubStrings, _FindSubStr.

classes.name: stzStringFormatter
classes.brief: Changes how a text looks: its case, its alignment and padding, its white space and its repetition.
classes.description: It is the formatting helper behind the case methods of stzString (Titlecased, CaseFolded...), which builds one over itself and writes the result back; reach for it directly with new stzStringFormatter(cText) or StzStringFormatterQ(cText) when you only need the formatting. Each Apply verb and each Align, Pad, Trim, Simplify and Repeat verb changes the held text in place and returns nothing (the Q form returns the formatter, so calls chain), and the past-tense form (Uppercased, RightAligned, Trimmed...) returns the new text and leaves the formatter alone. Read the result with Content. Widths and reversals count characters, not bytes, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji text is handled whole. Pass a plain text, not a stzString object: an edit through a formatter empties the stzString that was passed in. PaddedLeft and PaddedRight ignore their padding character; use PadLeft and PadRight.
classes.example:
? o1.Titlecased()
#--> Hello World
? "[" + o1.RightAligned(14) + "]"
#--> [   hello WORLD]
o1.PadRight(14, "*")
? o1.Content()
#--> hello WORLD***
o2 = new stzStringFormatter("שלום עולם")
? o2.NumberOfChars()
#--> 9
? o2.Reversed() = "םלוע םולש"
#--> 1
o3 = new stzStringFormatter("ab😀")
? "[" + o3.CenterAligned(7) + "]"
#--> [  ab😀  ]

classes.name: stzStringLeadTrail
classes.brief: Looks at the two ends of a text: runs of repeated characters, prefixes and suffixes to test, strip or make sure of.
classes.description: It is the helper behind the ends-of-a-string methods of stzString (RemoveRepeatedLeadingCharsCS, EnsurePrefixCS, RemoveFromStartCS...), which builds one over itself and writes the result back; reach for it directly with new stzStringLeadTrail(cText) when you only need the ends. The reads (RepeatedLeadingChars, StartsWith, LeadingChar...) answer a text, a number or TRUE or FALSE; the verbs (RemoveFromStart, EnsurePrefix, RemoveThisLeadingChar...) change the held text in place and return nothing, the Q form returning the helper so calls chain; the past-tense forms (RemovedFromStart, PrefixEnsured) return the new text and leave the helper alone. Read the result with Content. A run needs at least two identical characters: a single leading character is not repeated. Matching is case-sensitive by default; StartsWithCS, EndsWithCS, EnsurePrefixCS and EnsureSuffixCS honour a case flag, while RepeatedLeadingCharsCS, RepeatedTrailingCharsCS (and so the Has and Number forms built on them) ignore it, and RemoveFromStartCS and RemoveFromEndCS do nothing for a flag of 0 when the case differs. Positions count characters, not bytes, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji runs are measured as you expect. Pass a plain text, not a stzString object: an in-place edit through the helper empties the stzString that was passed in.
classes.example:
? o1.RepeatedLeadingChars()
#--> aaa
? o1.NumberOfRepeatedTrailingChars()
#--> 3
? o1.RepeatedLeadingCharsRemoved()
#--> abccc
o2 = new stzStringLeadTrail("example.com")
o2.EnsurePrefix("https://")
? o2.Content()
#--> https://example.com
o3 = new stzStringLeadTrail("םםםשלום!!")
? o3.NumberOfRepeatedLeadingChars()
#--> 3
o4 = new stzStringLeadTrail("😀😀😀ok😀😀")
? o4.RepeatedTrailingCharsRemoved() = "😀😀😀ok😀"
#--> 1

classes.name: stzStringList
classes.brief: Holds a list of strings and answers questions about it: find, count, sort, filter, replace, split and change case.
classes.description: Reach for it when the strings of a list are the subject and a stzList is more than you need. It checks at birth that every item is a string, and the per-string work goes to the engine. Methods such as Add, SortInAscending, Unique, ToUpper and Trim change the list in place; the Sorted, Uppercased and Trimmed forms return a plain Ring list and leave it alone. Search methods come in a case-sensitive form and a CS form that takes a flag, as in FindCS(pcStr, 0).

classes.name: stzStringLocale
classes.brief: Answers questions about a text that depend on its script, its reading direction and its locale.
classes.description: It wraps a stzString and asks the engine, which counts Unicode characters and not bytes. Case conversion takes a locale, so Turkish dotted and dotless i come out right. Script tests tell the writing system, and a text that mixes two of them, the shape of a homograph attack, is reported by IsMixedScript; digits and spaces never count as a script of their own there. Known limit today: Hebrew letters are not seen as right to left (see DetectDirection), and LocaleCompare orders by character with case ignored, not by the rules of a language.

classes.name: stzStringRemover
classes.brief: Deletes parts of a text: a substring, an occurrence, a position or section, the spaces, the repeats or what lies between two bounds.
classes.description: It is the removal helper behind many Remove methods of stzString, which builds one over itself and writes the result back; build one directly when you only need the removals. Each verb changes the held text in place and returns nothing (the Q form returns the remover so calls chain), and the form that ends in -Removed returns the new text and leaves the remover alone. Read the result with Content. Positions count characters, not bytes, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji text is cut where you expect. Pass a plain text, not a stzString object: editing through a remover empties the stzString that was passed in. The case-flag forms (CS) of the first, last, nth, from-left, from-right and between removals ignore their flag today, and the nth rank starts at 0 here. An end position before a start position, or a closing-bound removal (IB) that finds no pair, kills the Ring process.
classes.example:
o1.RemoveFirst("an")
? o1.Content()
#--> bana split
o2 = new stzStringRemover("שלום עולם")
o2.RemoveSpaces()
? o2.Content()
#--> שלוםעולם
o3 = new stzStringRemover("a😀b😀c")
? o3.CharRemovedAt(2)
#--> ab😀c

classes.name: stzStringReplacer
classes.brief: Substitutes parts of a text: a substring, an occurrence, a position, the characters of a set, a pair of bounds or a regex match.
classes.description: It is the substitution helper behind many Replace methods of stzString, which builds one over itself and writes the result back; build one directly when you only need the replacements. Each verb changes the held text in place and returns nothing (the Q form returns the replacer so calls chain), and the form in the past tense (Replaced, Surrounded) returns the new text and leaves the replacer alone. Read the result with Content. Positions count characters, not bytes, so Hebrew, Arabic and emoji text is cut where you expect, except in ReplaceByMany. Pass a plain text, not a stzString object: apart from Replace, an edit through a replacer empties the stzString that was passed in. The ranks of ReplaceNth start at 1 but the default RemoveNth starts at 0, RemoveFirst removes the second occurrence and RemoveLast removes nothing, unless the case flag is given as 0.
classes.example:
o1.Replace("world", "all")
? o1.Content()
#--> hello all
o2 = new stzStringReplacer("שלום עולם")
o2.Surround("«", "»")
? o2.Content()
#--> «שלום עולם»
o3 = new stzStringReplacer("a😀b😀c")
? o3.Replaced("😀", "-")
#--> a-b-c

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Builds a replacer over a text, given as a string or as a stzString object.

parameters.name: pStrOrStzStrObj
parameters.role: the text to edit, or a stzString whose content is edited

notes: pass a plain text and read the result with Content; stzString does it safely by writing the replacer result back with Update
warnings: with a stzString argument, Replace edits the stzString you passed in place, but every other edit (ReplaceFirst, Surround, ReplaceNth...) leaves the stzString you passed reading as an empty text; the replacer itself keeps the right text

classes.name: stzStringText
classes.brief: Answers questions about a text as prose: its words, sentences, paragraphs and lines, its writing systems, and common clean-ups.
classes.description: stzString builds one of these to answer Script, Words and the other text-level questions; build one directly with a text, or use stzText, which inherits from it and adds meaning-level methods. Words, sentences and lines follow the Unicode rules, so Hebrew, Arabic, Chinese and emoji text is segmented where a reader would expect. Verbs such as ReverseWords and Simplify change the held text in place and return nothing (the Q form returns the object so calls chain), and the past- tense form (WordsReversed, Simplified) returns the new text and leaves the object alone. Pass a plain text, not a stzString: the first edit made through the object empties the stzString that was passed in. Known defects today: UniqueWords keeps the punctuation stuck to a word, so ContainsWord misses it; ReverseEachWord and EachWordReversed break any non-ASCII word; OnlyScript, OnlyArabic and OnlyLatin raise errors; ToSentenceCase capitalizes only the first letter.
classes.receiver: o1 = new stzStringText("the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog")
classes.example:
? o1.NumberOfWords()
#--> 9
? o1.WordsReversed()
#--> dog lazy the over jumps fox brown quick the
o2 = new stzStringText("שלום עולם")
? o2.WordsReversed()
#--> עולם שלום
? o2.Script()
#--> hebrew
o3 = new stzStringText("Hello 😀 world مرحبا")
? o3.Script()
#--> hybrid
? o3.NumberOfWords()
#--> 3

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Builds a text object from a string or from a stzString, ready to be asked about its words, sentences, lines and scripts.

parameters.name: pStrOrStzStrObj
parameters.role: the text, or a stzString whose content is used

notes: pass a plain text and read the result with Content; stzText inherits from this class and adds meaning-level methods
warnings: with a stzString argument, the first edit made through the text object (Update, ReverseWords...) leaves the stzString you passed reading as an empty text, while the text object keeps the right text (two datasets)

methods.name: Content
methods.brief: Returns the whole text as one string.

methods.name: NumberOfChars
methods.brief: Returns how many characters the text holds, counting an emoji or a Hebrew letter as one.
notes: Hello followed by a blank and an emoji gives 7

methods.name: IsEmpty
methods.brief: TRUE if the text is empty.

methods.name: Copy
methods.brief: Returns a new, independent text object with the same content.
notes: changing the copy does not change the original

methods.name: ToStzString
methods.brief: Returns the same text wrapped as a stzString, for the character-level methods.

methods.name: Engine
methods.brief: Returns the handle of the engine string that holds the text.
notes: an internal handle for engine calls, not the text

methods.name: Update
methods.brief: Replaces the whole text by a new one.

parameters.name: pcStr
parameters.role: the new text, or a pair [ :With, text ]

methods.name: UpdateWith
methods.brief: Replaces the whole text by a new one.

parameters.name: pcStr
parameters.role: the new text, or a pair [ :With, text ]

notes: same effect as Update

methods.name: SetLanguage
methods.brief: Records the working language of the text, for the callers that ask for it.

parameters.name: pcLanguage
parameters.role: the language name, such as English

notes: the text itself is not analysed differently: nothing in this class reads the language

methods.name: Language
methods.brief: Returns the language set with SetLanguage.
methods.returns: the language given, or NULL when none was set

methods.name: Script
methods.brief: Returns the dominant writing system of the text, such as latin, arabic or hebrew.
methods.returns: a lower-case text; hybrid when several scripts are mixed
notes: digits and punctuation count as common, which is ignored when one real script is present: 12345 gives common, Hello 😀 world مرحبا gives hybrid
warnings: an empty text raises an error (Information about script is unavailable)

methods.name: Scripts
methods.brief: Returns the writing systems used by the text, in order of first appearance.
notes: the blank counts as common: the Hebrew text שלום עולם gives hebrew, common

methods.name: NumberOfScripts
methods.brief: Returns how many different writing systems the text uses.
notes: blanks and punctuation count as one more script, common

methods.name: CountScripts
methods.brief: Returns how many different writing systems the text uses.
notes: same answer as NumberOfScripts

methods.name: NumberOfDistinctScripts
methods.brief: Returns how many different writing systems the text uses.
notes: same answer as NumberOfScripts

methods.name: ScriptIs
methods.brief: TRUE if the dominant writing system of the text is the given one.

parameters.name: _cScript_
parameters.role: the script name, such as :Latin, :Hebrew or :Hybrid

methods.name: ContainsScript
methods.brief: TRUE if at least one character of the text belongs to the given writing system.

parameters.name: _cScript_
parameters.role: the script name, such as :Arabic

methods.name: ContainsArabicScript
methods.brief: TRUE if the text contains Arabic-script content.

methods.name: ContainsLatinScript
methods.brief: TRUE if the text contains Latin-script content.

methods.name: IsLatinScript
methods.brief: TRUE if the string is written in the Latin script.

methods.name: IsArabicScript
methods.brief: TRUE if the string is written in the Arabic script.

methods.name: IsHanScript
methods.brief: TRUE if the string is written in the Han script.

methods.name: IsHybridScript
methods.brief: TRUE if the string mixes several scripts.

methods.name: IsCommonScript
methods.brief: TRUE if the chars belong to the Common script.

methods.name: IsInheritedScript
methods.brief: TRUE if the chars belong to the Inherited script.

methods.name: OnlyScript
methods.brief: Raises error R24 today instead of returning the part of the text written in a given script.

parameters.name: pcScript
parameters.role: the script name to keep

notes: read the characters with ToStzString().Chars() and keep the ones you want meanwhile
warnings: raises Using uninitialized variable pcscript for :Latin, :Hebrew and :Arabic alike: the anonymous function it builds does not see its own parameter

methods.name: OnlyArabic
methods.brief: Raises error R14 today instead of returning the Arabic-script part of the text.
notes: read the characters with ToStzString().Chars() and keep the ones you want meanwhile
warnings: raises Calling Method without definition: concatenateq on a Latin text and on an Arabic text alike

methods.name: OnlyLatin
methods.brief: Raises error R14 today instead of returning the Latin-script part of the text.
notes: read the characters with ToStzString().Chars() and keep the ones you want meanwhile
warnings: raises Calling Method without definition: concatenateq on a Latin text and on a mixed text alike

methods.name: NumberOfWords
methods.brief: Returns how many words the text holds, by the Unicode word rules.
notes: punctuation and emoji are not words; each Chinese character is one word

methods.name: NthWord
methods.brief: Returns the word at the given rank, counted from 1.

parameters.name: _n_
parameters.role: the rank of the word, counted from 1

methods.returns: a text; an empty text when the rank is outside the text
notes: the second word of the quick brown fox is quick

methods.name: FirstWord
methods.brief: Returns the first word of the text.
methods.returns: a text; an empty text when there is no word

methods.name: LastWord
methods.brief: Returns the last word of the text.
methods.returns: a text; an empty text when there is no word

methods.name: Words
methods.brief: Returns the words of the text, in order, as a list.
methods.returns: a list of text; an empty list when there is no word
notes: punctuation is dropped: Hello world. gives Hello, world; WordsQ returns it as a stzList, WordsU keeps each word once and WordsZ pairs each word with its positions

extensions.name: WordsQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

extensions.name: WordsU
extensions.adds: returns the result without duplication

extensions.name: WordsZ
extensions.adds: includes the position in what it returns

extensions.name: WordsExcept
extensions.adds: takes exceptions, what to leave out

methods.name: UniqueWords
methods.brief: Returns each distinct word once, in order of first appearance, with the punctuation stuck to it.
notes: UniqueWordsCS(0) merges words that differ only by case
warnings: the words keep their neighbouring punctuation, so Hello world. Bye world, ok gives world. and world, as two different words, where Words gives world; ContainsWord, ContainsEachWord and NumberOfUniqueWords read this list and are wrong for the words that touch a punctuation mark

extensions.name: UniqueWordsCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

methods.name: NumberOfUniqueWords
methods.brief: Returns how many different words the text holds.
notes: the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog gives 8
warnings: counts the words with their stuck punctuation, as UniqueWords does: world. and world, are two

methods.name: IsWord
methods.brief: TRUE if the text is a single word.

methods.name: IsArabicWord
methods.brief: TRUE if the text is a single Arabic-script word.

methods.name: IsLatinWord
methods.brief: TRUE if the text is a single Latin-script word.

methods.name: ContainsWord
methods.brief: TRUE if the given word occurs as a whole word in the text.

parameters.name: pcWord
parameters.role: A word, as text.

notes: a part of a word is not a word: fo is not found in fox; ContainsWordCS("FOX", 0) ignores case
warnings: a word followed by a punctuation mark is not found: ContainsWord("world") is FALSE on Hello world. Bye, and ContainsWord("بالعالم") is FALSE on an Arabic sentence where that word is followed by a full stop; a non-text argument raises an error

extensions.name: ContainsWordCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

methods.name: ContainsNoWord
methods.brief: TRUE if the text contains NONE of the given words.

parameters.name: pcWord
parameters.role: A word, as text.

methods.name: ContainsEachWord
methods.brief: TRUE if every word of the given list occurs as a whole word in the text.

parameters.name: pacWords
parameters.role: the list of words that must all be present

warnings: it uses ContainsWord, so a word followed by a punctuation mark is not found

extensions.name: ContainsEachWordCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

methods.name: ReverseWords
methods.brief: Reverses the order of the words, in place, and joins them with single blanks.
methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. ReverseWordsQ returns the object for chaining
notes: the quick brown fox gives fox brown quick the, and one two three with extra blanks gives three two one

extensions.name: ReverseWordsQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: WordsReversed
methods.brief: Returns the text with the order of its words reversed, leaving the object unchanged.
notes: Hebrew and Arabic words keep their letters: שלום עולם gives עולם שלום

methods.name: SortWords
methods.brief: Sorts the words alphabetically, in place, with capitals first.
methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. SortWordsQ returns the object for chaining
notes: the order is by code point: The the THE cat Cat gives Cat THE The cat the, and SortWordsCS(0) ignores case and gives cat Cat The the THE

extensions.name: SortWordsCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

extensions.name: SortWordsCSQ
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag; does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

extensions.name: SortWordsQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: WordsSorted
methods.brief: Returns the words sorted alphabetically as one text, leaving the object unchanged.
notes: WordsSortedInAscending returns the same words as a list

extensions.name: WordsSortedCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

methods.name: ReverseEachWord
methods.brief: Corrupts any non-ASCII word today: it reverses the bytes of each word, in place, and the text ends up empty.
notes: reverse the letters of a Hebrew or Arabic word with stzStringCharList.Reversed meanwhile
warnings: on שלום עולם, on a😀 b and on été vert the text reads as empty afterwards, because a reversed byte sequence is not valid text; ASCII words are reversed correctly (the quick gives eht kciuq)

extensions.name: ReverseEachWordQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: EachWordReversed
methods.brief: Returns the text with the bytes of each word reversed, which is only right for ASCII words.
methods.returns: a text; garbled bytes for a word with non-ASCII characters
notes: same defect as ReverseEachWord
warnings: Hebrew, Arabic, emoji and accented words come back as unreadable bytes: été vert gives garbage followed by trev, while the quick gives eht kciuq

methods.name: RemoveNthWord
methods.brief: Deletes the word at the given rank, in place.

parameters.name: _n_
parameters.role: the rank of the word, counted from 1

methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. RemoveNthWordQ returns the object for chaining
notes: the quick brown fox with 2 gives the brown fox

extensions.name: RemoveNthWordQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: NthWordRemoved
methods.brief: Returns the text without the word at the given rank, leaving the object unchanged.

parameters.name: _n_
parameters.role: the rank of the word, counted from 1

methods.name: InsertWordAt
methods.brief: Inserts a word so that it takes the given rank, in place.

parameters.name: _n_
parameters.role: the rank the new word takes, counted from 1, 0 meaning the start

parameters.name: pcWord
parameters.role: the word to insert

methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. InsertWordAtQ returns the object for chaining
notes: Hello world with 2 and x gives Hello x world

extensions.name: InsertWordAtQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: SwapWords
methods.brief: Exchanges two words, given by their ranks, in place.

parameters.name: n1
parameters.role: the rank of the first word, counted from 1

parameters.name: n2
parameters.role: the rank of the second word

methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. SwapWordsQ returns the object for chaining
notes: the words are joined by single blanks afterwards

extensions.name: SwapWordsQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: TruncateWords
methods.brief: Keeps only the first words, in place.

parameters.name: _n_
parameters.role: how many words to keep

methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. TruncateWordsQ returns the object for chaining
notes: the quick brown fox with 3 gives the quick brown

extensions.name: TruncateWordsQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: WordsTruncated
methods.brief: Returns the first words of the text, leaving the object unchanged.

parameters.name: _n_
parameters.role: how many words to keep

methods.name: RemoveDuplicateWords
methods.brief: Deletes the words that already appeared earlier, keeping the first of each, in place.
methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. RemoveDuplicateWordsQ returns the object for chaining
notes: case counts: The the THE stay three words

extensions.name: RemoveDuplicateWordsQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: DuplicateWordsRemoved
methods.brief: Returns the text with each repeated word kept once, leaving the object unchanged.
notes: the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog loses its second the

methods.name: CountWordsMatching
methods.brief: Returns how many words in the text are exactly the given text.

parameters.name: pcPattern
parameters.role: the text a word must equal, case counted, taken as it is written and not as a regular expression

notes: a word stuck to a punctuation mark only matches with it
warnings: the pattern is compared with the blank-separated pieces of the text, punctuation included, and is not a regular expression or a wildcard: on Hello, World! hello again the pattern hello counts 1, Hello, counts 1 and [a-z]+, H* and ^again$ count 0

methods.name: NumberOfOccurrenceOfWord
methods.brief: Returns how many times the given word occurs as a whole word.

parameters.name: pcWord
parameters.role: A word, as text.

notes: punctuation next to the word does not matter, and a part of a word does not count: he is 0 in the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog, and the is 2; NumberOfOccurrenceOfWordCS("THE", 0) ignores case

extensions.name: NumberOfOccurrenceOfWordCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

methods.name: WordFrequency
methods.brief: Returns the share of the words of the text that are the given word, as a fraction between 0 and 1.

parameters.name: pcWord
parameters.role: the word whose share is wanted

methods.returns: a number such as 0.22 for the in the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog
notes: an absent word gives 0
warnings: raises an error on a text with no word; it returns one number for the word asked and does not pair every word with its frequency, which is WordsAndTheirFrequencies

methods.name: WordsAndTheirCounts
methods.brief: Returns each distinct word with the number of times it occurs, in order of first appearance.
methods.returns: a list of [ word, count ] pairs
notes: punctuation is dropped, and case counts: The the THE gives three entries, WordsAndTheirCountsCS(0) gives The with 3

extensions.name: WordsAndTheirCountsCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

methods.name: MostFrequentWords
methods.brief: Returns the most frequent words with their counts, the highest count first.

parameters.name: _n_
parameters.role: how many words to return

methods.returns: a list of [ word, count ] pairs, at most as many as asked
notes: the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog with 2 gives the with 2 and quick with 1

extensions.name: MostFrequentWordsCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

methods.name: WordsAndTheirFrequencies
methods.brief: Returns each distinct word with its share of all the words, in order of first appearance.
methods.returns: a list of [ word, fraction ] pairs; an empty list when there is no word
notes: the shares add up to 1

methods.name: MostFrequentWord
methods.brief: Returns the word that occurs most often, the first one met in case of a tie.
methods.returns: a text; an empty text when there is no word
notes: case counts: The the THE gives The

methods.name: LessFrequentWord
methods.brief: Returns the word that occurs least often, the first one met in case of a tie.
methods.returns: a text; an empty text when there is no word
notes: in the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog every word but the occurs once, so it gives quick

methods.name: NMostFrequentWords
methods.brief: Returns the most frequent words, without their counts, the highest count first.

parameters.name: _n_
parameters.role: how many words to return

methods.returns: a list of text, at most as many as asked
notes: the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog with 2 gives the and quick

methods.name: WordsPositions
methods.brief: Returns the start positions of every occurrence of every word, as one flat list in text order.
notes: the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog gives 1, 5, 11, 17, 21, 27, 32, 36, 41

methods.name: WordsAndTheirPositions
methods.brief: Returns each distinct word with the start positions of all its occurrences.
methods.returns: a list of [ word, positions ] pairs
notes: positions count characters, and the positions of a word are found without regard to case

methods.name: WordsSortingOrder
methods.brief: Returns the order in which the words already come: ascending, descending or unsorted.
methods.returns: a lower-case text: ascending, descending or unsorted
notes: the comparison is by code point, capitals first; apple banana cherry gives ascending

methods.name: WordsAreSorted
methods.brief: TRUE if the words are already in ascending or in descending order.
notes: one word or none counts as sorted

methods.name: WordsAreSortedInAscending
methods.brief: TRUE if each word comes before or equals the next, by code point.
notes: apple banana cherry answers TRUE; a capital comes before every small letter

methods.name: WordsAreSortedInDescending
methods.brief: TRUE if each word comes after or equals the next, by code point.
notes: cherry banana apple answers TRUE

methods.name: WordsSortedInAscending
methods.brief: Returns the words sorted from the smallest to the largest, as a list, leaving the text unchanged.
notes: repeated words are kept

methods.name: WordsSortedInDescending
methods.brief: Returns the words sorted from the largest to the smallest, as a list, leaving the text unchanged.
notes: repeated words are kept

methods.name: NumberOfSentences
methods.brief: Returns how many sentences the text holds, by the Unicode sentence rules.
notes: a full stop followed by a lower-case letter does not end a sentence

methods.name: Sentences
methods.brief: Returns the sentences of the text, in order, as a list.
methods.returns: a list of text; an empty list when the text is empty
notes: a line break also ends a sentence; Hello there. How are you? Fine! gives three

methods.name: NthSentence
methods.brief: Returns the sentence at the given rank, counted from 1.

parameters.name: _n_
parameters.role: the rank of the sentence, counted from 1

methods.name: FirstSentence
methods.brief: Returns the first sentence of the text.
methods.returns: a text; an empty text raises an error
notes: Hello there. How are you? Fine! gives Hello there.

methods.name: LastSentence
methods.brief: Returns the last sentence of the text.
methods.returns: a text; an empty text raises an error

methods.name: NumberOfParagraphs
methods.brief: Returns how many paragraphs the text holds, a paragraph being cut off by an empty line.
notes: a line holding only blanks does not cut a paragraph

methods.name: Paragraphs
methods.brief: Returns the paragraphs of the text, trimmed, as a list.
methods.returns: a list of text; an empty list when the text is empty
notes: the text is cut at each empty line, so line breaks stay inside a paragraph

methods.name: NthParagraph
methods.brief: Returns the paragraph at the given rank, counted from 1.

parameters.name: _n_
parameters.role: the rank of the paragraph, counted from 1

methods.name: FirstParagraph
methods.brief: Returns the first paragraph of the text.
methods.returns: a text; an empty text raises an error

methods.name: LastParagraph
methods.brief: Returns the last paragraph of the text.
methods.returns: a text; an empty text raises an error

methods.name: NumberOfLines
methods.brief: Returns how many lines the text holds.
notes: a final line break counts as one more, empty, line: hello, world and a line break give 3

methods.name: Lines
methods.brief: Returns the lines of the text, in order, as a list.
methods.returns: a list of text; the empty text gives one empty line
notes: empty lines are kept

methods.name: NthLine
methods.brief: Returns the line at the given rank, counted from 1.

parameters.name: _n_
parameters.role: the rank of the line, counted from 1

methods.returns: a text; an empty text when the rank is outside the text

methods.name: FirstLine
methods.brief: Returns the first line of the text.

methods.name: LastLine
methods.brief: Returns the last line of the text.
methods.returns: a text; empty when the text ends with a line break

methods.name: DeduplicateLines
methods.brief: Deletes the lines that already appeared earlier, keeping the first of each, in place.
methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. DeduplicateLinesQ returns the object for chaining
notes: case counts by default: one, One, one, two keeps one, One, two, and DeduplicateLinesCS(0) keeps one, two

extensions.name: DeduplicateLinesCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

extensions.name: DeduplicateLinesCSQ
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag; does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

extensions.name: DeduplicateLinesQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: LinesDeduplicated
methods.brief: Returns the text with each repeated line kept once, leaving the object unchanged.
notes: LinesDeduplicatedCS(0) ignores case

extensions.name: LinesDeduplicatedCS
extensions.adds: takes a case-sensitivity flag

methods.name: RemoveBlankLines
methods.brief: Deletes the empty lines and the lines holding only blanks, in place.
methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. RemoveBlankLinesQ returns the object for chaining
notes: the other lines keep their text and their order

extensions.name: RemoveBlankLinesQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: RemoveEmptyLines
methods.brief: Deletes the empty lines and the lines holding only blanks, in place.
methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. RemoveEmptyLinesQ returns the object for chaining
notes: same effect as RemoveBlankLines

extensions.name: RemoveEmptyLinesQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: BlankLinesRemoved
methods.brief: Returns the text without its empty and blank-only lines, leaving the object unchanged.

methods.name: NumberLines
methods.brief: Puts the line number and a colon in front of every line, in place.
methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. NumberLinesQ returns the object for chaining
notes: empty lines are numbered too: the first line becomes 1: followed by the line

extensions.name: NumberLinesQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: LinesNumbered
methods.brief: Returns the text with every line prefixed by its number and a colon, leaving the object unchanged.

methods.name: Simplify
methods.brief: Collapses every run of blanks, tabs and line breaks into one blank and trims the ends, in place.
methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. SimplifyQ returns the object for chaining
notes: line breaks go too: a, two tabs, b, two line breaks, c, two blanks and d gives a b c d

extensions.name: SimplifyQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: Simplified
methods.brief: Returns the text with every run of blanks, tabs and line breaks collapsed into one blank and the ends trimmed, leaving the object unchanged.

methods.name: CollapseSpaces
methods.brief: Collapses every run of blanks, tabs and line breaks into one blank and trims the ends, in place.
methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. CollapseSpacesQ returns the object for chaining
notes: line breaks go too, as with Simplify; two blanks, too, three blanks and many give too many

extensions.name: CollapseSpacesQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: SpacesCollapsed
methods.brief: Returns the text with every run of blanks, tabs and line breaks collapsed into one blank and the ends trimmed, leaving the object unchanged.

methods.name: NormalizeSpaces
methods.brief: Collapses the runs of blanks and tabs into one blank and trims the ends, keeping the line breaks, in place.
methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. NormalizeSpacesQ returns the object for chaining
notes: a, tabs, b, two line breaks, c, two blanks, d gives a b, the two line breaks, c d

extensions.name: NormalizeSpacesQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: SpacesNormalized
methods.brief: Returns a copy where each run of blanks or tabs is one blank and the ends are trimmed, line breaks kept.

methods.name: ToSentenceCase
methods.brief: Capitalizes the first letter of the text, in place.
methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. ToSentenceCaseQ returns the object for chaining
notes: the sentences it works on are the ones cut by the Unicode rules, which do not cut before a lower-case letter
warnings: the letters that start the later sentences stay as they are in the cases tried: one. two. three. gives One. two. three., hello world. this is it! and so on? yes gives Hello world. this is it! and so on? yes, and it works! really? yes. gives It works! really? yes.

extensions.name: ToSentenceCaseQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: SentenceCased
methods.brief: Returns the text with its first letter capitalized, leaving the object unchanged.
warnings: the later sentences are not capitalized in the cases tried, as with ToSentenceCase

methods.name: Pluralize
methods.brief: Turns the text into its English plural, in place, as if it were one word.
methods.returns: nothing; the text changes. PluralizeQ returns the object for chaining
notes: only regular English rules: city gives cities, box gives boxes, dog gives dogs, but child gives childs; a non-English word just receives an s

extensions.name: PluralizeQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: Pluralized
methods.brief: Returns the English plural of the text, leaving the object unchanged.
notes: the plural applies to the end of the text: the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog gives a text ending in dogs

methods.name: ToSlug
methods.brief: Returns the text as a URL slug: lower case, words joined by hyphens, and only ASCII letters and digits kept.
notes: Hello, World! gives hello-world
warnings: non-ASCII letters are dropped and not transliterated: Ça va très bien gives a-va- trs-bien, and Hebrew or Arabic text gives an empty text

methods.name: Abbreviate
methods.brief: Returns the text cut so that it fits the given length, ending in three dots, and does not change the text.

parameters.name: nMaxLen
parameters.role: the greatest length of the result, in characters

methods.returns: a text, at most nMaxLen characters long, the three dots included
notes: the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog with 10 gives the qui...; Hebrew is cut by characters
warnings: despite what its older description said, it does not change the object: read the answer, and call Update with it to keep it

methods.name: Initials
methods.brief: Returns the first letter of every word, joined in one text.
notes: the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog gives tqbfjotld and keeps the case; an emoji counts as a word here

methods.name: DiacriticsRemoved
methods.brief: Returns the text with its accents and other combining marks taken off, leaving the object unchanged.
notes: Café déjà vu, Ça gives Cafe deja vu, Ca

methods.name: RemoveDiacritics
methods.brief: Takes the accents and other combining marks off the text, in place.
notes: Café déjà vu, Ça becomes Cafe deja vu, Ca

methods.name: Lowercase
methods.brief: Changes the whole text to lower case, in place.

classes.name: stzSurfacePlot
classes.brief: Draws parts of a whole as a treemap whose cell areas are proportional to the values: as text, SVG or PNG.
classes.description: Despite its name it draws no function surface: it is a composition plot. The data is positive numbers, or label = number pairs, and the largest values get the largest cells. ToString draws box-drawing borders with a name centred in each cell; ToSVG and ToPNG draw coloured rectangles with the name and the share of the total, which :ShowValues = 0 removes. Setters answer the plot itself so calls can be chained, unlike the other plot classes. In the text picture a name wider than its cell is cut at both ends (Support reads upp.), values and percentages together run into each other, and in the pixel picture parts too small for a label get none; see the warnings. Gallery: doc/gallery/stzSurfacePlot/budget.png (five departments), seen right by stzlib-docs visual pass (a model reading the PNG), 2026-10-05, not a person; manyparts.png (twelve parts, seven with no label), seen uncertain by the same pass; terminal.txt is the text picture, read as text and judged wrong because a label is clipped.

classes.name: stzSystemCall
classes.brief: Runs an external program from a command line or from a program and a list of arguments, and keeps its output and exit code.
classes.description: Build the call, run it, then read Output, Error and ExitCode. The command is run by the engine with no console window. A list of arguments given with SetArgs reaches a program that is not a shell one by one, with no shell parsing them; a command line that starts with a shell word such as echo or holds a pipe is wrapped to run through the shell. ReturnType asks for the output as text, as lines or as a number. Set the program and arguments only from values you trust, since the call starts a real process.
classes.example:
o1.Run()
? o1.Succeeded()
#--> 1
? o1.OutputAsLines()[1]
#--> hello world
? o1.ExitCode()
#--> 0

classes.name: stzSystemProfile
classes.brief: Describes one system as a bundle of facts: its operating system, runtime, resources and capabilities.
classes.description: A profile is a named scope the code is written against. A live one (stzDevSystem, stzCurrentSystem) is filled from the machine; a declared one, made with DeclareSystem, holds only the values it was given, so a profile for Android answers android on a Windows machine. The capabilities are drawn from a closed list, and Forbids, Requires and CompareTo set a target against this system. A profile is saved to and read from a .stzsystem text file.
classes.example:
o1.SetOSName("android")
? o1.SystemClass()
#--> mobile
o1.SetCapabilityList([ "filesystem", "network", "clock" ])
? o1.Can("network")
#--> 1
? @@( o1.CapabilityKinds() )
#--> [ "effectful", "sensing" ]

classes.name: stzSystemScope
classes.brief: Checks feature code written for a deployment target: forbidden operations raise, operations the live machine lacks are rehearsed.
classes.description: A scope is the context feature code is written in. Each capability-tagged operation (ReadPin, Spawn, Connect, UseOp and the others) is compared with the target profile and with the live machine: the target forbids it, so an error is raised during development; the machine can do it, so it is native; the machine cannot, so it is rehearsed and kept for the lowering bridge. Nothing is performed: the scope classifies and records, it never runs the operation.

classes.name: stzTable
classes.brief: Holds a table of named columns and numbered rows, and answers questions about its cells, rows and columns.
classes.description: Reach for it when data has columns that deserve a name and rows that deserve a position. The content is stored column by column, as [ name, list of cells ] pairs, so a column is reached by its name (case does not matter) or by its position, and a row only by its position. A table is built from rows whose first line holds the column names, from rows alone (the columns are then called col1, col2 ...), from a hash list of name = cells pairs, or from a [ columns, rows ] size pair. Mutators change the table in place and return nothing; the CQ forms and the Sorted and Filled families give a result without touching it. The class inherits stzList, so a method not defined here falls through to the list. Many names are alternative spellings of one method, and a good share of the class is unfinished: about 200 methods raise an error or do nothing today, and each of them says so in its brief and its warning.

classes.name: stzTablex
classes.brief: Tests whether a stzTable fits a pattern written in a small regex-like language, such as {cols(3) & unique(name)}.
classes.description: A pattern is text in braces made of terms: cols, rows, col, row, cell, colname, hascol, property, contains, sorted, unique, duplicates, grouped, filtered, aggregated, transposed, calculated, coltype, colpattern, sumcol, avgcol, mincol, maxcol, nulls, completeness, numeric, alphabetic and format, written like cols(3) or sumcol(sales:>50000). Terms are joined by & (all must hold), a vertical bar (one must hold) and -> (a sequence), @! negates a term, @cs: makes it case-sensitive, and results are cached per pattern and table content. cols and rows take a number or a comparison: > and < are strict, >= and <= are at-least and at-most. A name the table does not have is simply not satisfied, it does not raise.

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Builds a table pattern from text such as {cols(3) & unique(name)} and parses it into tokens; a non-text value raises an error.

parameters.name: pcPattern
parameters.role: the pattern text, with or without braces

notes: the braces are added when missing; a term written without parentheses, such as {cols}, parses into a token with no constraint

methods.name: NormalizePattern
methods.brief: Trims the pattern text and wraps it in braces when it has none.

parameters.name: _cPattern_
parameters.role: the pattern text, with or without braces

methods.name: ParsePattern
methods.brief: Splits a braced pattern at its top-level -> into parts and parses each part into a token.

parameters.name: _cPattern_
parameters.role: the pattern text, with its braces

methods.returns: a list of tokens, each a list of [ key, value ] pairs; one token per part, so {cols(2) -> rows(1)} gives two
notes: a part joined by & or a vertical bar is ONE token, a conjunction or an alternation, holding its conditions

methods.name: SplitByOperator
methods.brief: Returns the parts of a text split at an operator that stands outside brackets.

parameters.name: cStr
parameters.role: the text to split

parameters.name: cOperator
parameters.role: the operator, such as "->"

methods.returns: a list of trimmed texts; "a->b->(c->d)" gives a, b and (c->d)
notes: an operator inside parentheses or braces does not split

methods.name: ParseAlternation
methods.brief: Parses a part whose terms are joined by a vertical bar into an alternation token holding the alternatives.

parameters.name: _cTokenStr_
parameters.role: the text of the part, with or without outer parentheses

methods.returns: a token: [ type, alternation ], [ alternatives, a list of tokens ] and [ negated, 0 ]

methods.name: ParseConjunction
methods.brief: Parses a part whose terms are joined by & into a conjunction token holding the conditions.

parameters.name: _cTokenStr_
parameters.role: the text of the part, with or without outer parentheses

methods.returns: a token: [ type, conjunction ], [ conditions, a list of tokens ] and [ negated, 0 ]

methods.name: ParseSingleToken
methods.brief: Parses one term such as unique(name) or @cs:contains(Ali) into a token: its type, value, constraints and flags.

parameters.name: _cTokenStr_
parameters.role: the text of one term

methods.returns: a token as a list of [ key, value ] pairs; [ ] for empty text; an ERROR token for a term it does not know
notes: @! sets negated, @cs: sets casesensitive, the quantifiers + * ? and n-m fill min and max, and Match never reads min and max; a term with no parentheses, such as cols, gets no constraint

methods.name: RemovePrefix
methods.brief: Removes the first of the given prefixes that the text starts with and returns the rest; the text is unchanged when none fits.

parameters.name: cStr
parameters.role: the text to shorten

parameters.name: aPrefixes
parameters.role: the prefixes to try, in order, as a list of text

notes: "@cols(3)" with [ "@cols", "cols" ] gives "(3)"

methods.name: ParseConstraints
methods.brief: Reads the text inside a term's parentheses into constraints: a number or comparison for cols and rows, a range or a set for cell.

parameters.name: cConstraintStr
parameters.role: the text to read

parameters.name: _cType_
parameters.role: the term type, such as cols, rows or cell

methods.returns: a list of constraints; [ ] for empty text, any other type, or a text it does not read, such as 2-5 for rows
notes: the greater and less forms are strict: cols(>4) is false for exactly 4 columns; the at-least and at-most forms are written >= and <=

parameters.name: oTable

classes.name: stzText
classes.brief: Holds a text as meaning rather than characters and answers natural-language questions about it: stems, tags, entities, tone, keywords, summaries, readability.
classes.description: A stzString is raw characters; a stzText carries meaning. It builds on stzStringText, which already gives Words, Sentences, the counts and the content, and adds the meaning layer, all computed by the engine: Snowball stemming in 25 languages and lemmatization in three, WordNet synonyms and hypernyms, VADER sentiment, Penn Treebank part-of-speech tags with chunking and a nested parse tree, rule-based named entities, stopwords and Flesch readability, RAKE key phrases, TextRank keywords and summaries, and language detection. Two groups upgrade themselves when a model is loaded for the process: the semantic group (Embedding, SemanticSimilarityWith, Classify, MostSimilarSentenceTo, NamedEntities) uses embeddings and a transformer NER head, and the generative pair (SummarizedAbstractively, AnswerAbout) asks a language model. With no model loaded they fall back to word overlap or answer an empty value, so a call never needs a model to run, with one exception noted on SummarizedAbstractively. The word-list methods work on one word or one sentence at a time and are only as good as the rule-based tagger. Known gaps today, each carried as a warning on its method: SummarizedAbstractively raises error R19 without a model, NamedEntities merges a capitalized word after a full stop into the previous entity, and EntityTypeOf and ClassifiedAs pick the first candidate on a tie.
classes.receiver: o1 = new stzText("The food was terrible. I love this wonderful place.")

classes.name: stzTime
classes.brief: Holds one time of day (hour, minute, second, millisecond) with no date, moves it around the clock, compares it and writes it in several formats.
classes.description: A stzTime is four numbers and never knows the day: adding 10 hours to 14:30 gives 00:30 and 23:00 is not before 01:00. Build it from a text (14:30, 14:30:15.250, 2:30 PM with a space before PM), from a number of seconds since midnight, from a hash with :Hour, :Minute, :Second and :Millisecond, or from an empty text for the clock now (the engine clock, which ran an hour behind Ring time() on this machine). The Add and Subtract methods move the object itself and answer the new HH:mm:ss text (the Q forms answer the object so calls chain); the Next and Previous methods answer a text and leave the object alone. Measure with SecsTo, MinutesTo and HoursTo, compare with IsBefore, IsAfter, IsEqualTo and IsBetween (to the second: the milliseconds are ignored), ask about the day with IsMorning, IsNight, IsWorkHours and PartOfDay, and write it with ToString, ToShort, ToLong or ToStringXT. Hours, Minutes, Seconds and Milliseconds are the parts of the time, not totals. Known gaps today, each carried as a warning on its method: To12Hour, ToSimple and the AP formats keep the 24-hour hour, ToHuman words the quarter-to wrongly at 11:45, 12:45, 23:45 and 00:45, ToRelative reads past as future, new stzTime(0) reads the clock, MSecsTo reads a time text as midnight, and the operators and comparisons refuse a time text such as 15:45 because StzIsTime accepts only one-digit parts.

methods.name: init
methods.brief: Builds the time of day from a time text, a number of seconds since midnight, a hash of parts, or the clock when the text is empty.

parameters.name: pTime
parameters.role: a time text such as 14:30:15.250 or 2:30 PM, a number of seconds since midnight such as 3661, a hash [ :Hour = 8, :Minute = 5, :Second = 9, :Millisecond = 45 ], or an empty text for now

notes: digits after a dot are a whole number of milliseconds, so .5 is 5 ms and .250 is 250 ms; an empty text reads the engine clock, which showed one hour less than Ring time() on this machine; hash keys are the singular :Hour, :Minute, :Second, :Millisecond and a missing one is 0
warnings: the number 0 reads the current clock instead of midnight (0 equals an empty text in Ring); a negative number or one of 86400 and more raises Invalid time provided!; a fraction of a second gives a broken second (01:01:1.50); a plain list [ 8, 5, 9 ] is ignored and gives 00:00:00; 2:30pm without a space before PM raises R41; hour 24, minute 60 and second 60 raise Invalid time provided!

methods.name: ParseStringTime
methods.brief: Sets the time from a text of hours and minutes, with seconds, milliseconds and AM or PM when present.

parameters.name: _cTime_
parameters.role: the time text, such as 07:45:10.500 or 3:15 PM, with a space before AM or PM

methods.returns: nothing; the object changes in place
notes: 12:xx AM becomes hour 0 and a PM hour below 12 gets 12 added; an hour of 13 or more with PM is kept as given
warnings: does not check ranges: 25:61:61 is stored and IsValid then answers FALSE; a text without two or three parts separated by : raises Cannot parse time string

parameters.name: _nSeconds_

notes: changes the object in place and keeps its milliseconds; 23:59:30 plus 45 seconds is 00:00:15; AddSecondsQ answers the object so calls chain
warnings: a fractional count leaves a fractional second in the object (12:00:0.50)

extensions.name: AddSecondsQ
extensions.adds: does what the method does, then returns the object, so the call can be chained

methods.name: operator
methods.brief: Applies one of the operators + - < <= > >= = between the time and a number of seconds or another time.

parameters.name: op
parameters.role: the operator text: + - < <= > >= =

parameters.name: v
parameters.role: the right-hand value: a number of seconds or a stzTime object

methods.returns: for + and - with a number, the object itself; for - with a stzTime, the signed seconds; for a comparison, TRUE or FALSE
notes: whole seconds only, the milliseconds are ignored
warnings: + and - change the object itself and answer it; time minus time is this minus the other, negative when this is earlier; a time text as right-hand value answers nothing for - and for every comparison (StzIsTime reads only one-digit parts), as do + with anything but a number and any other operator

methods.name: SecsTo
methods.brief: Returns the signed number of whole seconds from the time to another one, negative when the other is earlier.

parameters.name: _oOtherTime_
parameters.role: the other time: a stzTime object or a time text

methods.returns: a number of seconds; 4500 from 14:30:00 to 15:45:00
notes: works with a time text as well as an object
warnings: the day is not tracked: 23:00 to 01:00 is -79200, not 7200; milliseconds are ignored

methods.name: MSecsTo
methods.brief: Returns the signed number of milliseconds from the time to another one, negative when the other is earlier.

parameters.name: _oOtherTime_
parameters.role: the other time as a stzTime object

methods.returns: a number of milliseconds; 4484500 from 14:30:15.500 to 15:45:00
notes: the only distance that counts milliseconds
warnings: a time text is read as 00:00:00 (every text gives the same answer): the parameter is overwritten by the object being built before it is read

methods.name: MinutesTo
methods.brief: Returns the number of whole minutes from the time to another one, rounded down.

parameters.name: _oOtherTime_
parameters.role: the other time: a stzTime object or a time text

methods.returns: a number of minutes; 75 from 14:30:00 to 15:45:00
notes: built on SecsTo, so milliseconds are ignored
warnings: rounds down, so a negative distance of 330.25 minutes is -331

methods.name: HoursTo
methods.brief: Returns the number of whole hours from the time to another one, rounded down.

parameters.name: _oOtherTime_
parameters.role: the other time: a stzTime object or a time text

methods.returns: a number of hours; 1 from 14:30:00 to 15:45:00
notes: built on SecsTo, so milliseconds are ignored
warnings: rounds down, so -5.5 hours is -6

methods.name: IsBefore
methods.brief: TRUE if the time is strictly earlier than the other time within the day, compared to the second.

parameters.name: _oOtherTime_
parameters.role: the other time: a stzTime object or a time text

notes: the day is not tracked: 23:00 is not before 01:00
warnings: milliseconds are ignored, so 14:30:15.500 is equal to 14:30:15.900

methods.name: IsAfter
methods.brief: TRUE if the time is strictly later than the other time within the day, compared to the second.

parameters.name: _oOtherTime_
parameters.role: the other time: a stzTime object or a time text

methods.name: IsEqualTo
methods.brief: TRUE if both times are the same to the second.

parameters.name: _oOtherTime_
parameters.role: the other time: a stzTime object or a time text

methods.name: IsBetween
methods.brief: TRUE if the time is strictly after the start time and strictly before the end time, within the day.

parameters.name: _oStartTime_

classes.name: stzTimeLine
classes.brief: Holds a stretch of time with labelled points and labelled spans on it, and answers what is at a date, what overlaps, where the gaps are, and draws it in text.
classes.description: A timeline runs from a start to an end, both dates or dates with a time, and everything on it is kept as text such as "2024-02-14 10:00:00". A point is a single labelled moment; a span is a labelled stretch with a start and an end. Both must lie inside the timeline, and neither may touch the blocked points and blocked spans that reserve parts of it. Labels may repeat. Point labels are stored in capitals and are matched in any case, but a span label keeps the case it was given, and FindSpan, HasSpan, RemoveSpan and RenameSpanLabel compare in capitals, so a span added as "Alpha" cannot be found through them while Span, SpanStart, SpanEnd and SpanDuration, which compare exactly, can. Many alternative spellings exist (moment, instant, period). Durations are whole seconds. ToString draws the timeline with box characters and a table of dates. Known defects, each carried as a warning: HasMoment and its spellings recurse until the stack overflows; WhatsAt for a time of day matches nearly every span; Gaps and UncoveredPeriods are wrong when one span contains others, and UncoveredPeriods answers nothing for a timeline without spans; Distance works only for point labels.

methods.name: SetCheckFrequency
methods.brief: HOW LONG THE LOOP WAITS BETWEEN TICKS, in milliseconds.
methods.detail: It used to take anything. Zero was the dangerous one: _WaitTick does sleep(@checkFrequency / MS_PER_SECOND), so a frequency of 0 is no wait at all -- 200 idle iterations in 2ms instead of 2000, a loop spinning flat out on a knob whose entire job is to make it wait. A non-number was the confusing one: it survived the setter and raised R41 "Invalid numeric string" inside RunLoop, nowhere near the call that caused it. A refused value leaves the old one alone. Answering a bad value by destroying a good one is its own defect.

methods.name: SetPatience
methods.brief: HOW MANY consecutive idle iterations the loop tolerates before it stops.
methods.detail: A count, not a duration -- RunLoop compares it against _emptyLoopCount_. Zero is meaningful and is the default (PATIENCE_NONE, mirroring libuv's uv_run: return as soon as there is no work), so only negatives and non-numbers are refused.

methods.name: Train
methods.brief: paInputs = [ [x...] ... ], paTargets = [ [y...] ... ] THE TRAINING LOOP RUNS IN THE ENGINE (numeric phase 6, slice 3).
methods.detail: The plan's line for this phase says "rewire the trainer and logistic regression to use gradients rather than hand-derived updates". The measurement says otherwise, so this does something else and records why: 1. THE HAND-DERIVED GRADIENTS WERE ALREADY EXACT. Slice 1's autodiff tape was used to check them -- the honest use of an autodiff -- and on a 1-tanh-1-sigmoid network the two agree to eight decimals on every weight. There was no correctness debt here to pay off. 2. A TAPE IS SLOWER THAN DERIVED CODE FOR A FIXED ARCHITECTURE. Reverse mode earns its overhead when the expression is arbitrary; a dense MLP is not, and its derivative is known in closed form. 3. IT WOULD HAVE CHANGED THE ANSWERS. This trainer minimises binary cross-entropy for a sigmoid output while REPORTING squared error (see the delta rules below, kept verbatim in nn.zig). Rebuilding it around "the gradient of the reported loss" reintroduces the a(1-a) factor that the original comment records as strangling gradients into the constant-0.5 XOR saddle. So the tape stays where it belongs -- arbitrary objectives and L-BFGS -- and nn.zig is this same derivation, compiled. Measured on 400 samples x 10 features through a 16-8-1 network, 100 epochs: 11.14 s -> 0.06 s. THE DELTA RULES ARE UNCHANGED and are worth restating because they are a choice, not a detail: softmax + categorical cross-entropy -> delta = a - y, loss = -sum y*log(a) sigmoid + binary cross-entropy      -> delta = a - y, loss REPORTED as squared error anything else                       -> the squared-error derivative

classes.name: stzTSNE
classes.brief: Draws a map of high-dimensional samples in 2 dimensions in which points that are near in the data stay near, using t-SNE.
classes.description: Built for LOOKING at data, not for measuring it: the map is nonlinear, random and one-way, distances and cluster sizes in it mean nothing, and the perplexity changes the picture, so try two values. The usual pipeline is ReduceWithPCA(30) then Fit. The run is seeded: the same SetSeed gives the same embedding, a different one a different layout. Fit refuses a perplexity that is not below the number of samples, so small data needs SetPerplexity first (the default is 30). Ordinary t-SNE can place new rows with Transform only approximately; LearnMapping switches to the parametric variant, whose Transform is exact for the training rows. PreserveDensity adds a term that makes cluster size more readable, and LearnInverse trains a network that goes back from the map to the data. Trustworthiness is the witness that the picture invented no neighbours.
classes.example:
o1.SetPerplexity(3)
o1.SetIterations(120)
o1.Fit()
? o1.IsFitted()
#--> 1
? len(o1.Embedding())
#--> 12
? o1.Trustworthiness() > 0.5
#--> 1

methods.returns: a list of rows, each a list of numbers, like the table
notes: all zero but the corner, which is 3, for the 3 by 3 table above
warnings: Raises an error until Polish has run

parameters.name: pnRow
